major_concerns: Validators are treated as ground truth but their coverage/accuracy is unspecified — mislabeling could bias results.
Adversarial-intent generation methods are underspecified and could enable misuse if published without safeguards.
Dataset provenance and public-license status for vendor configs are not fully detailed; may affect reproducibility and legality.
Statistical power/sample-size justification for 600 paired tasks is not shown; uncertain sensitivity for primary McNemar test.
Exact model identifier, prompt templates, decoder/settings, and retry policy must be frozen and disclosed in preregistration.
required_design_repairs: Provide explicit validator specifications, test-coverage matrix, and validation correctness evaluation (e.g., validator-vs-expert spot checks).
Define and document adversarial-intent generation algorithm, redaction/safety policy for release, and mitigations for misuse.
Provide dataset provenance, licensing, and selection procedure for the 600 intents; include hashing/archival plan.
Add a pre-experiment power analysis to justify 600-task sample or adjust sample size.
Record and freeze exact model identifier(s), prompts, decoding parameters, random seeds, and retry policy in preregistration JSON.

major_concerns: Public release poses security risks (adversarial generators, validators) and needs a clear responsible-disclosure strategy.
Benchmark artefacts rely on hosted-model behaviour; reproducibility across time/providers requires archived outputs and deterministic seeds.
Metrics (rollback-worthiness score) need formal definition and validation against operational meaning.
Risk of benchmark overfitting by future systems if validators expose exploitable patterns.
Licensing and redistribution of vendor-derived configs and grammars is unspecified.
required_design_repairs: Define and formalize rollback-worthiness metric and its weighting scheme; justify operational relevance.
Specify responsible-release policy: what will be public, what will be redacted, and how to provide safe interfaces for validators/adversarial generators.
Include archival plan: store and publish model outputs, seeds, hashes to permit later verification despite provider drift.
Document licensing/rights for all dataset items; substitute or redact nonredistributable elements.
Pre-register model identifiers, per-task model-call cap, and reproducibility-run protocol (number of repeats, seeds).

major_concerns: Constructing correct vendor grammars and parsers is labor-intensive; risk of incomplete grammars biasing results.
Neurosymbolic repair rules may introduce unanticipated semantic changes that validators do not detect.
Integration with constrained-decode hooks may require model/API features not universally available; portability concerns.
Latency and operational cost of repair pipeline may make results academically interesting but operationally impractical without latency targets.
required_design_repairs: Provide concrete plan and tooling for grammar construction, parser validation, and coverage tests (e.g., corpus-driven grammar completeness metrics).
Specify the repair-rule provenance, test-suite for rule correctness, and detection of repair-induced regressions.
Confirm availability of decoding hooks or describe fallback approach if hosted API lacks needed controls.
Predefine acceptable latency thresholds and measure cost-per-decision; include practical deployment constraints in evaluation.

major_concerns: Detailed adversarial payloads and exploitation patterns could be misused if published without mitigation/redaction.
Simulated attacks may not reflect real adversary capabilities; external validity must be bounded.
Definition of 'attack success' conflates semantic validator-failures with successful malicious insertion; needs clear taxonomy.
Ethical/legal constraints on crafting attack payloads and publishing examples must be addressed.
required_design_repairs: Adopt a responsible-disclosure policy: redact exploit payloads in public artifacts, provide safe summarized exemplars, and offer validator-only interfaces where needed.
Define attacker threat model explicitly (capabilities, access level) and justify representativeness.
Formalize attack-success definitions and map them to operationally meaningful outcomes (e.g., unauthorized config change vs. benign syntax noise).
Confirm experiments run only in simulation; include attestations and logs proving no live-device executions and detail safeguards used.
